sources.title: Beyond Clearing: Central Counterparties’ Investment and Risk Management of Cash from Margin Calls
sources.source_note: Primary research source supplied as the published IMF working paper. IMF Working Papers represent research in progress and do not necessarily represent IMF institutional views. VALO records source-supported findings separately from VALO inference and does not republish the full third-party paper.

evidence.proposition: The mere presence of a human in the loop is not sufficient to constitute meaningful human involvement or intervention; the person must be sufficiently informed and independent to reach an objective view not improperly influenced by the automated decision.
Human oversight can fail because people may be unable to scrutinise AI outputs effectively and may over-rely on automated outputs through automation bias.
evidence.evidence_type: committee finding based on witness evidence

evidence.proposition: AI systems posing a high risk of causing harm to human rights should require prior approval before they are provided or deployed.
Obligations should be distributed across the AI lifecycle and supply chain so risks are addressed by actors positioned to identify and prevent them.
Mandatory transparency should include disclosure that AI is being used, what it is being used for, and information about data sources when AI may significantly affect people or communities.
Central counterparties can incur material non-default losses from investing cash received through margin calls and default-fund contributions, even when no clearing member defaults.
For the CCP sample studied, market risk on direct investments is generally contained, while counterparty credit risk in reverse-repo exposures can be material for a subset of CCPs.

Low, zero or negative reverse-repo haircuts can leave CCP cash exposures insufficiently protected against collateral depreciation if a counterparty defaults; the paper finds non-positive haircuts are rarely justified under plausible risk assumptions.

Estimated reverse-repo counterparty-credit losses are modest relative to invested cash in most cases but can consume a significant share of CCP own resources; the paper reports an NDL-style Cover-2 measure reaching about 13 percent of the default fund in the most exposed cases.

evidence.locator: Conclusions and Avenues for further work, pages 24-25
evidence.proposition: Investment-related non-default losses can transmit stress through recovery and loss-allocation mechanisms to clearing members and the wider market ecosystem, supporting the need for better observation of effective haircuts, repo terms and recovery transmission paths.

claims.text: Human presence in an AI workflow is not, by itself, evidence of effective human control.
For high-risk AI, deployment approval and the legitimacy of later operation are distinct questions.
Effective challenge and remedy require case-relevant information about AI use, not only a general description of a system.
A system designed to absorb a primary risk can create a materially different downstream risk through what it does with resources after the primary control point.
Nominal collateralization is not sufficient evidence of protected economic effect when haircut calibration, counterparty failure and collateral-value changes can create residual loss.
Risk mitigation can redistribute risk into liquidity, counterparty, concentration or recovery channels rather than eliminate it.

analysis.text: Governance should distinguish representation of control from evidence of control. Policies, approval states and human-in-the-loop labels describe intended governance but do not by themselves prove that a concrete consequential action was legitimate and effectively controllable when it occurred.

The IMF CCP case supports a general resource-lifecycle analysis pattern: verify not only the boundary where a resource is accepted or protected, but also subsequent transformation, reuse, new exposure, realized consequence and downstream loss allocation. A safe-node or protected-resource representation is not equivalent to evidence of safe realized behavior.
